title: Africa doesn’t just need more startups. It needs ways to help viable businesses survive
gist: A WEF Global Shapers essay argues Africa's binding SME constraint is not business formation but business continuity: commercially viable, founder-dependent firms in Nigeria and similar high-migration economies are liquidated piecemeal when owners emigrate, retire or burn out. The proposed fix is a small-ticket ($10k–$50k) 'entrepreneurship through acquisition' market funded partly by diaspora capital, which requires purpose-built 'trust infrastructure' — verified listings, prospective revenue verification via digital payments, escrow, and handover periods — rather than a copy of the US $14.4m-median search fund model.

themes.theme: Continuity gap, not a startup gap

insights.claim: The binding constraint on African SME development is business continuity rather than business formation: viable enterprises are shut down when owners relocate, retire, burn out or face personal shocks, destroying jobs, supplier relationships and customer networks alongside the founder's income.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Development capital and donor programmes aimed almost entirely at startup incubation may be mis-allocated; the higher-return intervention is transfer and succession plumbing for already-cash-generating firms.
insights.quote: The current frontier of SME development is business continuity: helping good businesses outlast their founders.
insights.locator: Africa does not only need more businesses

insights.claim: Business failure in high-migration African markets is frequently a transferability failure rather than a commercial failure — the author closed a consultancy serving clients across Africa, the EU and the UK not because it lost money but because ownership could not be handed over.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Standard SME mortality statistics conflate two very different causes; underwriting models that treat all closures as credit-quality signals will mis-price viable founder-dependent businesses.
insights.quote: It had not failed in the commercial sense. It simply could not transfer.
insights.locator: Not long after, I found myself

insights.claim: Consumer 'declutter pages' listing industrial ovens, bread pans, commercial mixers, freezers and salon equipment are a real-time leading indicator of small-business liquidation, because dismantled firms are sold as separate assets rather than as going concerns.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Scraping second-hand commercial-equipment listings is a cheap, high-frequency alternative dataset for tracking informal-sector distress and emigration waves where official registry data lags.
insights.quote: The business was not being sold as a going concern. Its assets were being broken up and sold piece by piece.
insights.locator: These were not just household clear-outs

insights.claim: Selling a firm as scrap assets rather than as an operating business destroys the intangible value — supplier terms, customer networks, staff — that constitutes most of a small firm's worth, so the continuity gap is a systematic value-destruction mechanism, not just an ownership inconvenience.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Any platform that converts piecemeal asset liquidation into going-concern sales captures a large arbitrage between scrap value and enterprise value.
insights.locator: It can mean lost jobs, broken supplier relationships

insights.claim: PwC, citing a 2021 national survey, puts Nigerian micro, small and medium-sized enterprises at 96.9% of businesses, 87.9% of employment and 46.32% of GDP — meaning nearly half of Nigerian output sits in firms structurally exposed to founder departure.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Emigration of skilled Nigerian founders is a macro-relevant shock channel, not a micro one; brain-drain metrics should be read as a direct drag on ~46% of GDP and ~88% of employment.
insights.quote: such enterprises account for 96.9% of businesses, 87.9% of employment and 46.32% of GDP
insights.locator: In Nigeria, micro, small and medium-sized enterprises

insights.claim: Founder dependency in African small firms is informational, not just managerial: records are informal, processes undocumented and customer and supplier relationships live largely in the owner's head, so there is no practical continuation pathway when the owner leaves.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Digital bookkeeping and POS adoption are not just efficiency plays — they are the precondition for any secondary market in small African businesses, expanding the addressable market for SME fintech.
insights.locator: Yet many of these firms remain deeply dependent

insights.claim: In many small firms the owner simultaneously holds every critical function, so a transfer must be engineered as a process — handover periods, management documentation, staged payments, local operator partnerships or seller advisory roles — rather than a single closing event.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Deal structures with earn-outs and mandatory seller transition periods are the default, not the exception, in this asset class; investors pricing clean cash-at-close exits will be disappointed.
insights.quote: The owner is the salesperson, operator, bookkeeper, negotiator and reputational anchor.
insights.locator: There is also the challenge of owner dependency

themes.theme: Redirecting diaspora capital from consumption to ownership

insights.claim: The World Bank estimated remittances to sub-Saharan Africa at about $54 billion in 2023, with Nigeria accounting for roughly a third of those flows — a pool larger than most regional development-finance budgets but almost entirely aimed at consumption.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Even a low-single-digit reallocation of a $54bn annual flow toward equity acquisition would dwarf existing African SME private-equity dry powder — a large latent TAM for remittance and investment platforms.
insights.quote: the World Bank estimated that remittances to sub-Saharan Africa reached about $54 billion in 2023, with Nigeria accounting for roughly a third of those flows
insights.locator: Remittances remain a major source of external finance

insights.claim: Remittances are overwhelmingly directed at consumption, education, healthcare, housing and family support and are not structured to preserve operating businesses, so the diaspora currently funds households while businesses in the same communities are liquidated.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The framing challenges the standard 'remittances are development finance' narrative; the investable opportunity is the missing product layer that converts transfer flows into productive ownership stakes.
insights.locator: But remittances are overwhelmingly directed at consumption

insights.claim: Small-business transfer infrastructure would create a 'return entrepreneurship' pathway in which diaspora investors and local operators acquire businesses that already serve communities instead of starting from scratch.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Watch for acquisition-oriented diaspora vehicles as a distinct category from the venture-style Africa funds that dominate today's capital stack.
insights.locator: It could also create new pathways for return entrepreneurship

themes.theme: Why the US search fund model doesn't port

insights.claim: Stanford's 2024 Search Fund Study covers 681 search funds formed in the US and Canada since 1984 and reports a recent median purchase price of $14.4 million — roughly three orders of magnitude above the relevant African small-business transfer size.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The unit economics of US-style search funds (expensive diligence, banker-led processes) cannot be transplanted; any African ETA vehicle must be re-engineered around a fee budget two to three orders of magnitude lower.
insights.quote: Stanford’s study reported a recent median purchase price of $14.4 million for search-acquired companies.
insights.locator: But African markets cannot simply copy

insights.claim: The author's own early market-sizing work in Nigeria points to a target acquisition band of roughly $10,000 to $50,000 per business — a ticket size at which conventional due diligence, legal and valuation costs would consume the entire deal.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: This is the key economic constraint: only a standardized, largely automated diligence-and-escrow product can make sub-$50k acquisitions viable, which favours platform businesses over advisory firms.
insights.quote: Early market-sizing work I have conducted in Nigeria focuses on a potential acquisition band of about $10,000 to $50,000.
insights.locator: In many African small-business transfer contexts

insights.claim: Because many prospective buyers are physically outside the country, an African ETA market must solve simultaneously for distance, trust, accountability and cross-currency financing — constraints absent from the domestic US search fund template.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Cross-currency settlement and remote verification are the hard technical moats here, pointing to fintech and payments incumbents rather than brokerages as the natural platform owners.
insights.locator: And because many buyers may be outside the country

themes.theme: Trust infrastructure as the missing product

insights.claim: The missing piece is not a listings marketplace but 'trust infrastructure' — verified listings, standardized business profiles, basic financial tracking, customer and supplier references, site visits, legal templates, escrow arrangements and vetted accountants, lawyers and valuers.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A pure classifieds play will fail; the defensible business is the verification-and-escrow stack, which is also where recurring take-rate revenue sits.
insights.quote: What is needed is not only a marketplace, but trust infrastructure.

insights.claim: For informal firms, prospective verification — tracking revenue through digital payments or point-of-sale systems over a defined period — is more useful than reconstructing imperfect historical financial statements.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: This inverts standard diligence and makes POS and payments providers the de facto credit and valuation bureaus for African SMEs — a strong strategic argument for their data assets.
insights.quote: Prospective verification – for example, tracking revenue through digital payments or point-of-sale systems over a defined period – may be more useful than trying to reconstruct imperfect historical records.
insights.locator: For more informal firms, retrospective financial statements

insights.claim: The design target for small-business transfer systems should be 'enough trust for responsible transactions', not perfect certainty — an explicit tolerance for residual risk that keeps verification costs inside a sub-$50k deal budget.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating such platforms should benchmark diligence cost per deal against expected loss rates rather than against developed-market diligence standards.
insights.quote: The objective is not perfect certainty, but rather enough trust for responsible transactions to happen.
insights.locator: The objective is not perfect certainty

insights.claim: Trust, not capital or demand, is presented as the load-bearing asset in African small enterprise: the author's teenage Lagos babysitting business survived a handover to a sibling purely because the parents' trust in the family transferred with it.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Implies that transfers within trusted networks (family, diaspora kin, known local operators) will clear far earlier than open-market listings — the wedge for any platform is closed communities first.
insights.quote: The business survived because the trust around it survived.
insights.locator: At the time, I did not think of this

insights.claim: Governments should act as enablers rather than builders — improving business registries, supporting digital financial records, clarifying transfer procedures, enabling secure escrow mechanisms and reducing friction around small-company ownership changes in partnership with private platforms, banks, law firms and SME agencies.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Registry digitization and escrow legislation are the concrete policy catalysts to watch; their arrival in a given market would be the trigger for private transfer platforms to scale there.
insights.quote: Governments have a role to play, but they do not need to build everything themselves.
insights.locator: Governments have a role to play

insights.claim: Beyond capital preservation, a functioning transfer market would let founders exit with dignity instead of dismantling what they built, keeping clinics, schools, workshops and small manufacturers open as service infrastructure in their communities.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Frames SME continuity as social-infrastructure resilience, which broadens the funding pool to impact and blended-finance investors, not just commercial acquirers.
insights.quote: A bakery should not disappear because its owner emigrates. A clinic should not close because its founder retires.
insights.locator: Africa does not only need more businesses
